parameterNotes.mergeThreads: one merge thread per search node, which is why the burst is six threads rather than one: the same merge ran on every member because every member held a copy of the segment.
parameterNotes.mergeSegments: how many segments the reindex left behind for the compactor to merge in one pass, which is the trigger the ticket names and the reason the burst was this wide.

groundTruth.rootCauseReason: The nightly reindex left forty-one segments for the compactor, and the merge that followed held every merge thread on all six search nodes at 98 % utilisation for four minutes. Nothing was killed and no limit was reached: the box gave the merge the CPU it asked for, which meant it gave it to nothing else. Query lag went from 1.2s to 84s, catalog-service carried that lag out to the storefront as a p99 of 300ms instead of 40ms, and then the merges finished and the numbers returned on their own. That recovery is the reason this case exists in the corpus: a saturation with a declared end is a different shape from one that lasts the window, and the corpus could not state it until `hold` existed -- every series it could write either held for all eight post-onset samples or for exactly one.

rootCauseIndicators.description: every merge thread at 98 % of the core it runs on, for four post-onset samples and then back to 12 %
query lag on the cluster risen from 1.2s to 84s and returned, which is the window the burst occupied rather than the window the incident occupied
the same four minutes seen one hop out, at 300ms against a 40ms baseline

causalChain.mechanism: the merge held every search thread it could schedule, so a query waited behind the merge instead of between merges: lag on the cluster rose from 1.2s to 84s for as long as the burst ran
catalog-service waits on search for every listing it renders, so the cluster's lag reached the storefront as its own query p99 -- 40ms to 300ms -- and left it when the merges finished

evidenceCheckpoints.description: the merge threads at 98 % of a core, which is the saturation itself rather than its effect on a query
query lag at the peak of the burst, seventy times the baseline the same series states before the onset
the p99 one hop out, which is what the storefront's users were served while the merge ran
the burst's own duration, cited from the injection's parameter rather than counted from prose, because the recovery is the claim this case is in the corpus to make
no request failed at any point, which is what separates a saturation that is slow from one that is also down

remediation.action: run the reindex's merges under their own CPU quota, or throttle the merge rate, so a routine compaction cannot take the threads a query needs
alarm on merge-thread utilisation as well as on query lag, so the next burst is a page before it is a fourteen-minute investigation

query: At 14:12 UTC query lag across the index went from 1.2s to 84s and stayed there for four minutes, while every merge thread on the six nodes running it sat at 98% utilisation, up from its usual 12%. catalog-service passed the delay on to the storefront as a p99 of 300ms, up from 40ms. No request failed, no pod restarted, and the numbers came back on their own. What saturated, and why did it clear itself?
